title: The form p*lice is under arrest
summary: Hour-long rant against the online 'form police', the commenters who correct other people's lifting form without being asked. NH argues that form depends on the individual's leverages, that hypertrophy depends on the distance travelled under tension rather than end positions (ATG depth, lockout, top squeeze), and that the form police ignore real form errors like stiff-leg RDLs, nose-level overhead presses and wall-backed curls. He closes by attacking the opposite anti-form dogmatism as well and argues for a logical middle ground.
claims: The form police are people who correct strangers' lifting form online without being asked, and they help no one
Unsolicited form tips are rarely welcome even in real life; NH tried correcting people in commercial gyms and they disliked it
Most online form critics don't lift and don't understand biomechanics
There is no universal form: proper technique depends on the individual's leverages, so proper form for one person is not proper for another
General technique pointers that suit most people exist, but they are flexible guidelines, not absolute rules
The form-policing mindset comes from powerlifting judging, which is legitimately strict but only applies inside competition
Bodybuilding went too far the other way and some bodybuilders pass off unsafe practices as effective; debate with powerlifters about this is healthy
For hypertrophy, range of motion means the distance the load travels under tension, not where the movement ends
A tall lifter squatting to parallel can travel more distance than a short lifter squatting ass to grass, so end depth alone doesn't measure ROM
Some people physically cannot squat ass to grass because of long femurs; it is a leverage limit, not a mobility problem
Pushing tall lifters to squat ATG despite heavy butt wink can lead to lower back injuries
Any knee-flexion squat is a squat; depth does not decide whether it counts
Olympic lifters squat extremely deep because their sport requires it, and they also dive-bomb and allow knee valgus for maximal power
Knee valgus or a 1RM dive-bomb may be acceptable for an athlete, but bodybuilders do many reps, so valgus harms tendons and the negative must be controlled because that is where hypertrophy occurs
At equal load and reps a deeper squat activates more muscle, but you usually move more weight to parallel; squat as deep as your leverages allow without limiting progression
Use both ATG and parallel squats: ROM is a variable in the specificity tree, and two ROMs give double progression
A 350 lb parallel squat may give better muscle activation than a 300 lb ATG squat
The form police are nearly always skinny: their uniforms only come in size S
Squat depth is very hard to judge from a video; serious powerlifting meets use three or more judges from different angles
Comments on NH's squat videos misjudged his depth every time, telling him to go deeper even when his glutes were folded onto his hamstrings
More ROM isn't always better: by that logic you'd deadlift from a trench or bench with a cambered spider bar, which would tear your pecs
Form policing comes from insecurity and a wish to feel superior, disguised as concern for injury
In years of commercial gyms nobody ever corrected NH's form, because people saw he was bigger than them
Strength sports give no style points: if a technique like sumo is in the rules and works, it counts
A 900 lb squat with slight knee cave beats a perfect 600 lb squat because the weight on the bar is what matters
The form-police style traces back to Elgintensity, who earned the right to be strict by lifting well and showing his face; anonymous critics have no standing
A half rep is still a rep; partial reps are not zero
Locking out a lift matters only for competition rules and safety; it contributes maybe 1% to hypertrophy
Squeezing at the top or thrusting the hips at the top of a squat or deadlift does nothing: with stacked joints the muscle is not under tension
At the top of a curl the weight rests on stacked bones, so the top squeeze gives no tension
NH is a form stickler himself: a rounding lumbar spine on deadlifts or a good-morning squat is bad form
On the overhead press the bottom range, shoulders flexed under load, matters most; starting at nose level is about 5x worse than not locking out
NH starts his overhead press with the bar at mid-chest for a full bottom range
Doing only small partials at the bottom of a lift wouldn't build big muscles either; the whole distance travelled counts
An RDL is a negative-only deadlift with bent knees as a hip hinge, not a stiff-leg movement; lower until the plates kiss the floor
Deadlifts that start above the knee skip the hardest part of the range and make the lift about twice as easy
Bouncing the bench, dive-bombing squats and touch-and-go deadlifts cheat the hardest part of the range; bodybuilders should control the negative
So-called strict curls with the back against a wall and raised elbows become a supported front raise rather than a curl
Removing part of the ROM reduces the hypertrophic effect but doesn't cancel it; partial pull-ups can build a big back, arguably better than full ones
Calling someone an ego lifter is mostly an ad hominem against heavy lifting; squatting ATG because the internet bullied you into it is the real ego lifting
Cheating lets you move more weight and strict form targets muscles; both are tools for progression
With dumbbells too big to clear the leg, a small hip movement on curls is not cheating
The bottom of a curl is mostly shoulder; the biceps work once the elbow is flexed, and fully straightening the arm under load risks a biceps tear
Dogmatic old-school channels like Rippetoe's spread the idea that there is only one way to lift
Gym-fail compilations are mostly watched by non-lifters who enjoy others' injuries
Wraps and sleeves add maybe 10-20 lb and are largely placebo unless very rigid
The anti-form reaction, typified by Bubble Brigade fanboys, is just as dogmatic; novices need structure, and that advice suits intermediates
The truth lies in the middle: some technique rules apply, but they must be adapted to the individual, not treated as absolute
exercises: more activation at equal load but usually less weight
allows heavier loads; combine with ATG for double progression
shows depth depends on biomechanics and sport
start bar at mid-chest; lockout optional
bottom range with shoulders flexed is most stimulating
bend the knees, hip hinge, negative only, plates kiss floor
don't skip below-knee portion; no touch-and-go for bodybuilding
no wall support, elbows down, don't straighten arm fully under load
bottom is mostly shoulder; biceps tear risk
